question: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room. What evidence did you bring, and when did you stop arguing?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project I pushed to use a simpler logging approach instead of the team's default. I pulled the last two sprints' incident data showing 40% of time was spent parsing logs and brought a one-page comparison of the two options. After the team lead walked through their scaling concerns I dropped it and switched to documenting the current approach better.
The scaling numbers they showed were from production traffic I hadn't seen yet, so I asked for the doc link and moved on.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room. What evidence did you bring, and when did you stop arguing?
Role: new grad on first team project
Situation: wanted simpler logging; brought sprint incident data and one-page comparison
Actions: presented numbers, listened to scaling counter-data, asked for doc and dropped it
Outcome: documented current approach instead; quote: 'The scaling numbers they showed were from production traffic I hadn't seen yet'
Follow-up: What made you stop? -> acknowledged missing context and moved on
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at junior level. The candidate described pushing a concrete alternative with their own data on a scoped task, then stopping once higher-context evidence appeared. Quote: 'The scaling numbers they showed were from production traffic I hadn't seen yet.' This shows ownership of their input plus coachability when new facts surfaced. The story stays local to one project with no over-claim on impact. Biggest strength is the clean stop condition tied directly to the evidence gap.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the team their API design was wrong because it didn't match what I learned in school. I kept bringing it up in standups until the tech lead told me to just implement what was spec'd.
Mostly the textbook patterns and that it felt cleaner. I didn't have any metrics from our service.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room...
Situation: disagreed with API design on first project
Actions: repeatedly cited school patterns in standups with no service data
Outcome: told to follow spec; quote: 'Mostly the textbook patterns and that it felt cleaner'
Follow-up: What evidence did you share? -> admitted no metrics from the actual service
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Challenge skillfully at junior level. The candidate argued from external textbook knowledge without tying it to team metrics or constraints and continued after clear direction. Quote: 'Mostly the textbook patterns and that it felt cleaner.' No evidence of adjusting when new information appeared. The story shows persistence without ownership of the outcome or learning from the pushback. Biggest gap is the absence of any stop condition or data from the actual system.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were about to launch overlapping features that would create duplicate customer workflows. I pulled usage data from both services plus support ticket volume and presented a merged roadmap in the joint planning meeting. After the other team's PM showed their Q3 commitment to execs I agreed to deprioritize my side and instead contributed review capacity to their launch.
How did you decide the tradeoff?
Their exec commitment and the ticket volume numbers made the overlap cost higher than I had modeled, so I shifted to review help.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room...
Situation: overlapping features across two teams creating duplicate workflows
Actions: aggregated usage + ticket data, proposed merged roadmap in joint meeting
Outcome: deprioritized own feature after seeing exec commitments; quote: 'Their exec commitment and the ticket volume numbers made the overlap cost higher than I had modeled'
Follow-up: How did you decide the tradeoff? -> adjusted based on cross-team constraints
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at senior level. The candidate used cross-team data to surface duplication risk and then adjusted scope once the other team's hard commitments surfaced. Quote: 'Their exec commitment and the ticket volume numbers made the overlap cost higher than I had modeled.' Story shows influence across teams without authority and a clear evidence-based stop. Scope is larger than individual work yet still grounded. Biggest strength is the tradeoff decision tied to visible constraints rather than personal preference.

lowerTranscript.text: I kept pushing in the planning meeting that my service should own the new capability because it was architecturally cleaner. The other team had already staffed it so I escalated to the director.
Mostly diagrams and that it would reduce future tech debt. No customer or cost numbers from either team.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room...
Situation: capability ownership dispute between teams
Actions: argued architectural cleanliness and escalated when outstaffed
Outcome: no resolution mentioned; quote: 'Mostly diagrams and that it would reduce future tech debt'
Follow-up: What data did you bring? -> no customer or cost metrics
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Challenge skillfully at senior level. The candidate escalated without customer or cost data and framed the argument around architecture alone. Quote: 'Mostly diagrams and that it would reduce future tech debt.' No evidence of adjusting position when team capacity facts appeared. Story lacks cross-team leverage or measurable impact. Biggest gap is the missing stop condition and reliance on escalation instead of data-driven influence.

raiseTranscript.text: We were six months into a market expansion that the board had approved when new regulatory signals made the original timeline unrealistic. I brought the updated compliance timeline plus three scenario P&Ls to the exec team and recommended pausing two regions. After the CFO showed the cash runway impact of a full pause I shifted the recommendation to a phased approach with one region delayed and the others proceeding under tighter controls.
The runway math showed a full pause would force a later re-entry at higher cost, so I traded scope for speed on the viable regions.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you backed yourself against a room...
Situation: regulatory signals conflicting with board-approved timeline
Actions: prepared compliance timeline + three scenario P&Ls, recommended pause
Outcome: adjusted to phased rollout after runway data; quote: 'The runway math showed a full pause would force a later re-entry at higher cost'
Follow-up: What changed your view? -> traded scope based on cash impact
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Challenge skillfully at exec level. The candidate surfaced a strategic conflict with board-level implications using scenario financials and then revised the recommendation when runway constraints were quantified. Quote: 'The runway math showed a full pause would force a later re-entry at higher cost.' Story demonstrates long-term trade-off thinking and leverage across finance and compliance. Scope is org-level with clear ambiguity. Biggest strength is the evidence-driven pivot that preserved optionality rather than forcing the original position.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the board the expansion plan needed to change because of new risks and kept pushing for a full stop until they agreed to review it again.
High-level risk slides and my assessment that the timeline was aggressive. No updated financial models or alternative scenarios.

Story shows persistence without strategic trade-off analysis. Biggest gap is the absence of scenario modeling or long-term leverage considerations.
